title: Confession rites
hookLine: from the Orthodox confession before an icon to the general confession in a prayer book

lines: SIDE BY SIDE, BEFORE AN ICON.
A STOLE OVER A BOWED HEAD.
cards: In a small Orthodox church, a woman stands at a lectern near the front, facing an icon of Christ, with a Gospel book and a cross resting there. The priest stands beside her, not across from her. She speaks quietly.
When she's finished, she bows her head, and he lays the end of his stole over it and prays.
Across town, in a church with a prayer book in every pew, a whole congregation kneels, and every voice says the same words at once: "We have left undone those things which we ought to have done."

teach.b: Christians confess in different rooms, leaning on the same two lines. The first comes one verse after yesterday's oil: "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed."

In James, confession is spoken out loud to another person. The second is from the first letter of John: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Now, three rooms. First, the Orthodox.

The person confessing stands before an icon of Christ, the priest beside them, and in some Orthodox prayers before confession the priest describes himself as only a witness: it's Christ who hears and forgives.
Second, the Catholic sacrament of penance, often called reconciliation. A person tells their sins to a priest in private, behind a screen or face to face, and hears the words of absolution.
The priest is bound by the seal of confession: he may never repeat what he heard.

Third, the general confession, said together from the old English prayer book: "We have left undone those things which we ought to have done; And we have done those things which we ought not to have done."

Some Protestant services include a prayer of confession like it, followed by words of forgiveness. Notice the order: left undone comes first, the good nobody got around to, the visit, the apology, the help.
In every room the shape is the same. Say it out loud. Hear that it's forgiven.

how: Orthodox Christians confess before an icon of Christ with a priest beside them; Catholics confess privately to a priest in the sacrament of penance and receive absolution; Anglican, Lutheran and some other Protestant services include a general confession said together, followed by a declaration of forgiveness.

games.q: you've wronged a friend in your church, and you're reading the letter of James. what does it tell you to do?
o: say nothing and hope it fades.
confess your faults one to another, and pray for one another.
wait for your friend to bring it up first.
games.why: "confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed." in James, confession is spoken, and it heals.

practice: Don't make a list; look for just one thing, something you did, or, following the prayer book, something you left undone: the call you didn't make, the thank-you never said.

Name it plainly to yourself, without excuses and without piling on. If you pray, bring it to God and rest on John's promise, faithful and just to forgive; if you don't, let it be named, and notice what changes when it is.

wordCard.voice: Confession rites. The church's ways of saying sin out loud and hearing it forgiven: before an icon, to a priest, or all together.

orig.note: Greek: confess, the verb in James 5:16, telling believers to confess to one another.
